levers.label: Own solar
levers.what: Your own solar, co-located with the battery. Fill it and charge the battery from it instead of the market.
levers.why: Own solar replaces bought charging power (about ₹2.2/kWh) and sells its surplus at midday prices, against about ₹4 cr of capex per MWac. The first MW lower the price a lot; past the size that fills the battery the surplus sells for less than it costs, and the price turns up again. This is the lever the optimiser sets.

levers.label: Battery energy
levers.what: Battery energy per contracted MW. The tender needs at least 2 (2 hours at full power).
levers.why: More than 2 MWh per MW buys headroom for degradation and bad days, but it is capex (about ₹1 cr per MWh) that earns nothing on a normal day, so the price rises. Below 2 is not allowed.

levers.label: Extra battery for evening sale
levers.what: Battery beyond the tender's 2 MWh per MW, kept for selling in the evening hours outside your two peak hours, once the day's commitment is met.
levers.why: It earns the market price on those evenings (the Pool does not settle it) but costs capex, O&M, augmentation and charging power. It lowers the price only when the evening hours left after your peak pay more than that cost over 15 years.

levers.label: Principal moratorium
levers.what: Years after the COD in which only interest is paid, no principal (the moratorium).
levers.why: Later principal means more cash to the equity in the early years, which the IRR values most, so the price falls slightly.

levers.label: Battery capex (all-in)
levers.what: All-in battery capex per MWh: cells, PCS, civil, EMS, everything up to the pooling station.
levers.why: The largest single cost of the bid: 200 MWh at ₹1 cr is ₹200 cr of the project. Every ₹0.01 cr per MWh is ₹2 cr of capex to recover over 15 years, so the price moves almost one to one with it.

levers.label: Target equity IRR
levers.what: The return your equity asks for, after tax. The strike price is solved so that the equity earns exactly this.
levers.why: The price is the direct answer to this number: a higher target needs a higher price. If you can live with a lower return, this is the cheapest rupee to find on bid day.

levers.label: Debt share
levers.what: The share of the project cost funded by loans; the rest is your equity.
levers.why: Debt at 9% is cheaper than equity at 14%, so more debt lowers the price, until the DSCR falls below what the lender accepts.

levers.label: Receivable days
levers.what: Days between selling the energy and receiving the money, which sets the working capital you must fund.
levers.why: More days tie up more cash at the working-capital interest rate, so the price rises a little.

levers.label: Plant availability
levers.what: The share of the daily 2 MWh per MW you expect to deliver, after outages and curtailment.
levers.why: Energy not delivered earns nothing and, beyond 10% a week, is penalised; so lower availability needs a higher price on the energy you do deliver.

levers.label: Pre-operative & IDC
levers.what: Pre-operative expenses and interest during construction, as a share of the hard cost.
levers.why: Added to the project cost before a unit is sold, so a higher share means a higher price.

levers.label: Transmission to the ISTS substation
levers.what: The line and bay from the plant to the ISTS substation, per contracted MW.
levers.why: A fixed cost of the connection; dearer evacuation means a higher price.

levers.label: Battery O&M
levers.what: Battery operation and maintenance per MWh a year.
levers.why: A yearly cost on the whole battery for 15 years; higher O&M, higher price.

levers.label: Scheduling, forecasting, fees, admin
levers.what: Scheduling and forecasting, exchange membership, SECI's administration, audit and other fixed costs, per contracted MW a year.
levers.why: A yearly fixed cost over the term; higher means a higher price.

levers.label: Insurance
levers.what: Insurance as a share of the capex each year.
levers.why: A yearly cost on the whole project; higher means a higher price.

levers.label: Battery degradation
levers.what: How much usable battery capacity is lost each year before augmentation tops it up.
levers.why: Faster fade means more augmentation (new cells bought every year to keep the 2 MWh per MW), so the price rises.

levers.label: Battery round-trip efficiency (AC)
levers.what: Round-trip efficiency of the battery: the energy out for every unit put in.
levers.why: At 87% you buy or generate 1.15 units for every unit sold; a better battery needs less charging power, so the price falls.

levers.label: O&M escalation
levers.what: How fast the O&M and fixed costs rise each year.
levers.why: The revenue is fixed at the strike price for 15 years, so costs that rise faster need a higher price from day one.

levers.label: Solar capex
levers.what: Solar capex per MWac, with domestic cells and modules as the RfS requires.
levers.why: Paid on every MW of own solar; dearer solar means a higher price, in proportion to the solar in the bid.

levers.label: RE generation commissioned
levers.what: When your own solar and wind come online, in months after the SCD. The tender allows up to 21 months after the SCD (36 from the Effective Date).
levers.why: Every month without own RE, the battery is charged entirely from the market at about ₹2.2/kWh; earlier RE replaces that cost sooner, so the price falls.

levers.label: Battery price fall (augmentation)
levers.what: How fast battery prices fall each year, which sets what the yearly augmentation (replacing faded capacity) costs.
levers.why: Faster falling prices make the later top-ups cheaper, so the price falls a little.

levers.label: Interest rate
levers.what: The interest rate on the senior loan.
levers.why: Paid on about three quarters of the project cost for the tenor; a cheaper loan lowers the price.

levers.label: Charges on group-company power
levers.what: Charges on group-company power: transmission and losses.
levers.why: Paid on every unit of group RE used for charging; higher charges, dearer charging, higher price.

levers.label: Group-company RE price
levers.what: The price of RE bought from your group companies to charge the battery, allowed after month 36 for up to 50% of the energy.
levers.why: Group RE replaces market power when it is cheaper; a dearer group price means more market power or dearer charging, so the price rises.

levers.label: Exchange fee on energy sold
levers.what: The exchange's fee on every unit you sell.
levers.why: Paid on the contracted supply and the surplus alike; a small lever.

levers.label: Charges on green-market power
levers.what: What you pay on top of the exchange price for green-market power: exchange fee, transmission charges and losses.
levers.why: It is paid on every unit bought for charging, all of it in the first years and a quarter later; higher charges mean dearer charging, so the price rises.

levers.label: Solar CUF (AC)
levers.what: Capacity utilisation of your solar, on the AC side: the share of the year it runs at full power.
levers.why: A better site makes more energy from the same capex: more free charging and more surplus to sell, so the price falls.

levers.label: Solar degradation
levers.what: How much the solar output falls each year.
levers.why: Faster degradation means less own energy in the later years, more bought power and less surplus sold, so the price rises slightly.

levers.label: Battery power
levers.what: Battery power per contracted MW. At least 1, so the battery can deliver the full MW in each peak hour.
levers.why: More power than 1 MW per MW only lets the battery charge or discharge faster; it costs inverters and earns almost nothing on this tender, so the price barely moves.

levers.label: Solar O&M
levers.what: Solar O&M per MW a year.
levers.why: A yearly cost on the own solar; higher O&M, higher price, in proportion to the solar in the bid.

levers.label: Market price escalation
levers.what: How the exchange prices move each year from today's IEX year, for both the midday charging price and the evening selling price (the F.9 path can split the two).
levers.why: Higher prices make charging dearer but the surplus you sell dearer too; which wins depends on how much surplus RE the bid sells. On the benchmark bid the surplus wins, so higher escalation lowers the price.

levers.label: REC price
levers.what: The price of a Renewable Energy Certificate. Energy sold in the brown markets (DAM, RTM) earns RECs; you keep half the proceeds.
levers.why: Extra income on the energy sold, so a higher REC price lowers the strike price a little.

levers.label: Bank guarantee cost (EMD, PBG)
levers.what: What the bank charges each year for the EMD and the performance bank guarantee.
levers.why: A small cost before and around the SCD; a small lever.

levers.label: Corporate tax
levers.what: Corporate tax on the project's profit (25.17% under section 115BAA).
levers.why: A higher tax rate needs a higher price for the same after-tax return; the early years carry little tax because of depreciation.

levers.label: Letter of Credit cost
levers.what: What the bank charges each year for the Letter of Credit SECI asks for (2000 × MW × (₹10 − strike price) × 30 days).
levers.why: The LC is larger the lower your strike price; its cost is small, so this lever barely moves the price.

verdict.text: At ₹8.33 the quote sits at the evening market (₹8.30 in the two chosen hours): the Pool is about neutral on your 100 MW (₹0.2 cr a year paid), so the corpus carries the full 500 MW at the price year's prices; on a lower evening view SECI would weigh the gap.

risks.title: Deviation settlement (DSM): about ₹0.2 cr a year
Availability: each 1% below the declaration costs ₹0.61 cr a year of revenue
SECI-designated hours: the two hours you would choose pay ₹8.30/kWh, the evening on average ₹6.73
Exchange, transaction and scheduling charges: ₹0.14 cr a year at ₹0.02/kWh
Weekly shortfall penalty: 1.5 × (₹10.00 − ₹8.32) on energy beyond 10% short
A part award, or none: SECI sizes the award to the corpus at the discovered tariff
Not yours: the evening price over 15 years

findings.detail: ₹209 cr of charging power over the term, mostly group RE at ₹2.50/kWh; own solar at ₹3.60 cr/MWac costs more per unit charged. The price is carried by the battery and the financing, not the sourcing.

findings.title: What carries the ₹8.32: the battery's capex ₹3.15/kWh, then charging power and exchange fees ₹1.99
findings.detail: Capex annualised at 10% over 15 years, costs averaged over the term, all over the energy supplied (70.8 GWh a year): the battery's capex ₹3.15; charging power and exchange fees ₹1.99; O&M, insurance, fixed costs and the LC ₹1.08; transmission, SECI's charges and pre-operative cost ₹0.81; own RE capex ₹0.67; augmentation ₹0.31; less surplus sales and RECs ₹0.02; the rest, ₹0.33, is tax and the return above the discount rate (the 13.0% equity target on 25% equity at 8.75% debt). The biggest line is where the price moves most.

findings.title: Green-market charging reaches 25.0% of the supply after month 36 (limit 25%)
findings.detail: Close to the cap, a dear day or a thin GDAM leaves the battery short. More own RE, or group RE within its 50% limit, gives room.

findings.title: A strike price of ₹19.92/kWh is 3.3× the highest FDRE peak-power award
findings.detail: Assured peak supply, 6000 MWh awarded ₹5.99–6.00/kWh for 4 hours of assured evening supply over 25 years. The CfD asks 2 hours for 15 years and pays through the market, so a quote far above those awards will not clear the auction. Find what carries the price in the findings below, then size again.

findings.title: At ₹19.92 the Pool pays about ₹62 cr a year for your 150 MW; the full 500 MW would need ₹206 cr a year against a ₹76 cr corpus
findings.detail: Amendment-04 (RfS 42.2.b) lets SECI restrict the capacity awarded to what the CfD corpus can carry at the discovered tariff. The Pool's pay-out is the strike price less the evening market price on every kWh settled (₹8.70/kWh average MCP in your two best evening hours at the price year); the lower the strike price, the more of the 500 MW SECI can afford to award. A bid near the market price needs little from the Pool and is the one most likely to be awarded in full.

findings.title: Own solar is not at its best: 29 MWac instead of 14 lowers the screening price by ₹3.970/kWh
findings.detail: The own-RE size was a first guess, not the optimiser's for these inputs. Run Optimise own RE on the Size step: it tries every size and keeps the one with the least strike price with every day met. Charging bought over the term: ₹117 cr.

findings.title: Little own RE (14 MWac for 150 MW): nearly all charging power is bought
findings.detail: ₹117 cr of charging power over the term at the green-market and group prices. Own solar charges the battery at what the plant costs you (about ₹2.2/kWh on the benchmarks) and sells its surplus; the optimiser finds the size where that beats buying.

findings.title: What carries the ₹19.92: the battery's capex ₹12.11/kWh, then O&M, insurance, fixed costs and the LC ₹2.53
findings.detail: Capex annualised at 10% over 15 years, costs averaged over the term, all over the energy supplied (58.6 GWh a year): the battery's capex ₹12.11; O&M, insurance, fixed costs and the LC ₹2.53; transmission, SECI's charges and pre-operative cost ₹1.79; charging power and exchange fees ₹1.35; own RE capex ₹1.26; augmentation ₹1.20; less surplus sales and RECs ₹0.03; the rest, ₹-0.29, is tax and the return above the discount rate (the 16.0% equity target on 25% equity at 9.00% debt). The biggest line is where the price moves most.

findings.title: The extra battery for evening sale (1.00 MWh/MW, 150 MWh) costs ₹25.5 cr a year and earns ₹0.0 cr
findings.detail: ₹180 cr of capex annualised at 10% over 15 years plus O&M, against its evening sales net of charging (average over the term: 0.0 GWh a year). It sells only once the day's commitment is met and within what the green-market limit leaves, which here is little. Set it to 0 unless the evening prices justify it.

findings.title: The battery fades below the need: the last year supplies 43.7% of the mandate
findings.detail: Augmentation is "annual" with 2.0% a year of fade; from operating year 2 the usable energy no longer covers 2 MWh per MW. Augment every year, add years to the schedule, or size the nameplate for the last year. At a strike price above the evening market the weekly penalty is nil, but the energy not supplied earns nothing and the price must rise to pay the plant.

findings.title: 1 input far from the benchmark in the direction that raises the price
findings.detail: Battery capex (all-in): 1.20 ₹ cr/MWh against 1.00 (+20%). Each is yours to set; the What-if step says what each is worth on the price. Keep the ones you have evidence for and freeze them there.

findings.title: Minimum DSCR 1.02× is below the lender's 1.10×
findings.detail: The debt as structured does not finance in its weakest year. Sculpt the repayment to the lender's DSCR (Finance inputs › Repayment), take less debt or a longer tenor, or accept a higher price; the lender's minimum is 1.10× and the model's lowest year gives 1.02×.

findings.title: A 16.0% equity IRR target is high for a contracted supply
findings.detail: SECI's recent awards price at 13–15% equity returns; every point of equity IRR is on the strike price. The benchmark is 14%.
